catasterism: For slaying the Gorgon and freeing Andromeda, Perseus was lifted into the heavens — still clutching Medusa's severed head, whose one open eye winks at us as the star Algol.
Rescued from the rock and the rising sea, Andromeda was set in the sky beside the hero who saved her and the parents who almost lost her — a family gathered again among the stars.
Her boast doomed her daughter, so the sea-god bound proud Cassiopeia to her throne and hung it at the pole — circling forever, half the night tipped upside-down as a lesson in humility.
The grieving king was placed in the sky beside his queen and rescued daughter, a quiet little house of stars keeping watch near the pole.
The sea-beast sent for Andromeda was turned to stone by the Gorgon's gaze and cast into the heavens, left to lap at the watery quarter of the sky.
Sprung from the Gorgon's blood and tamed to carry heroes, the winged horse was given a stall among the stars by Zeus — who keeps him there to bear the thunderbolts.
After his twelve labours and a mortal, painful end, Heracles was taken up to Olympus and set in the sky kneeling, one foot resting on the head of the dragon he once slew.
The invulnerable lion that Heracles strangled with bare hands was raised into the sky by Zeus, so the first and fiercest of the labours would never be forgotten.
Sent by Hera to nip the hero's heel and crushed for its trouble, the little crab was lifted gently into the sky by the goddess — a small reward for a loyal failure.
The many-headed serpent of the marsh, burned away head by head, was stretched out across the south as the longest creature in all the sky.
Ladon, the sleepless dragon that guarded the golden apples, was coiled by Hera around the pole when he fell — set where the stars never set, so he might guard the heavens still.
The jewelled crown Dionysus gave Ariadne was flung skyward on their wedding night, and each gem caught and stayed — a small, perfect ring of light.
For its lie and its dawdling, Apollo cast the crow into the sky beside the cup it can never reach, the water-snake forever in the way.
Apollo set the cup in the heavens beside the thirsty crow and the coiling snake — a still goblet of stars held just out of reach.
The arrow loosed to free Prometheus was laid to rest among the stars, a slender dart resting between the eagle and the swan.
Zeus's eagle — bearer of his thunderbolts and of the young cupbearer Ganymede — was given a place of honour, climbing the summer Milky Way.
On this altar the gods swore their pact before the war with the Titans; in victory they set it in the sky, its drifting smoke becoming the Milky Way.
Asclepius, the healer who learned to raise the dead, was struck down by a wary Zeus — then placed in the sky with his serpent, so his gentle art would not be wholly lost.
The serpent of healing, shedding its skin to be born anew, is held forever in the steady hands of the sky's physician.
Wise Chiron, wounded past all healing, gave up his immortality so Prometheus might go free — and was set among the stars as the noblest of the centaurs.
The golden ram that carried two frightened children to safety gave up its fleece and was raised to the sky, the bright herald that leads in the spring.
When mortal Castor fell, his twin Pollux begged to share his own immortality rather than live without him — so Zeus set the brothers side by side, never to be parted.
The keel of the great ship Argo, her impossible voyage done, was laid to rest in the southern sky — anchored by Canopus, second-brightest of all the stars.
The stern of the Argo was set among the southern stars, the deck where fifty heroes once stood now sailing the Milky Way.
The sails of the Argo were spread across the southern sky, catching a wind that never falls.
The dove that Jason loosed to test the Clashing Rocks flew through and lived — and was placed in the sky near the ship she guided safely on.
The wise archer who first drew a bow was raised to the heavens, his arrow held forever at the Scorpion's heart, guarding the hunter's memory.
A wreath laid down by the centaur was set quietly beneath his feet — a small southern crown resting in the Milky Way.
Ganymede, the boy Zeus loved and carried up to Olympus, pours the water of the gods forever from his jar across the sky.
The sea-goat who blew the conch that scattered the Titans — goat above, fish below — was set among the stars by a grateful Zeus.
The swan that glides down the Milky Way: the shape Zeus once took, and the very swan, some say, that Orpheus became — laid at last beside his lyre.
Aphrodite and her son leapt into the river as two fish, their tails tied so they would never lose each other — and so, tied still, they swim the sky together.
Callisto, turned to a bear and nearly slain by her own son, was swept up into the sky by Zeus — caught by the tail, which is why the Great Bear's tail is so long.
Her son Arcas was set beside her as the Little Bear, the two circling the pole together — lifted high so the jealous sea could never pull them under.
The herdsman who drives the bears around the pole was given his own place among the stars — some say young Arcas, some the kind farmer Icarius and his faithful hound.
The little foal Celeris, swift brother of Pegasus, peeks over the edge of the sky — only his head was ever set among the stars.
Stung dead by the scorpion he never saw, Orion was set among the winter stars — and his small killer placed at the sky's far side, so hunter and scorpion never share the night.
The little scorpion that felled the boastful hunter was honoured with a place in the sky, where it rises only once Orion has safely set.
Orion's great hound followed his master into the sky and would not leave his heel, its eye the brightest star in all the night — Sirius.
The hunter's smaller dog trots beside him still, marked by faithful Procyon, who rises just ahead of the Dog Star to announce him.
The hare that bolts beneath Orion's feet was set in the sky as the hunter's quarry — forever a leap ahead of his two hounds.
The great bull — Zeus in disguise, who carried Europa across the sea — lowers his horns at Orion across the winter sky, the Pleiades riding his shoulder.
After Orpheus was lost, the Muses begged Zeus to lift his lyre into the heavens — so that its music, at least, would never quite leave the world.
Erichthonius, who first yoked horses to a chariot, was set in the sky by Athena — the mother-goat Capella tucked warm against his shoulder.
The dolphin that carried the drowning poet Arion safe to shore — and later won Amphitrite for Poseidon — was set among the stars as thanks for its kindness.
Down this long celestial river fell Phaethon, scorched from the sun-chariot he could not steer — its waters winding away into the southern dark.
Astraea, maiden of justice, was the last of the gods to leave a darkening world — and took her place in the sky, the wheat-ear Spica still bright in her hand.
Once the reaching claws of the Scorpion, these stars were re-imagined as the scales of justice, balanced in the hands of Virgo at his side.
The Great Fish lifts its mouth to drink the stream poured endlessly from Aquarius's jar, marked by the lonely southern beacon Fomalhaut.
